name: Story Night: a family story circle on the TV
pitch: A Vega OS app for one evening activity. Each phone in the room joins by scanning a QR code. One phone photographs an old print, and the photo fills the TV. The elder telling the story speaks into their own phone. Everyone else sends follow-up questions privately from their phones. The person holding the remote picks the next question with the D-pad. The session becomes a 'family episode' that keeps the teller's voice, adds captions and replays on the TV. When two tellers remember the same photo differently, the app records both versions with attribution and shows the conflict as a question for the family. The model never decides which version is right.
primary_user: Households where three to eight people of different generations share one living room: grandparents, parents and children. An adult child usually organizes. Indian joint families and visiting diaspora families are the first segment (assumption).
problem_frequency: Episodic: gatherings, festivals and visits. Estimated at monthly or less. This is an assumption and has not been measured.
problem_severity: Low urgency but irreversible. A story is lost when the teller dies. Emotional value is high and functional value is low. This is inference, not measured.
current_workaround: Asynchronous services: Remento ($99/yr; voice prompts sent by email or SMS, made into a printed book) and Storyworth ($99/yr; weekly written prompts). Two-person recording apps: Willow and StoryCorps (free; archive at the Library of Congress). Families also cast photos to the TV or send WhatsApp voice notes. No tool reviewed runs a group session around a shared screen.

demand_evidence.claim: A review written by a competitor says people want to 'sit together and have the conversation in person' and criticizes Storyworth because it is 'designed for one person responding alone'.
demand_evidence.quality: Low to medium. Vendor-authored and conflicted (Willow promotes its own product). It shows a stated preference, not measured demand.

demand_evidence.claim: Remento claims '1M+ stories recorded' and sells a $99/yr voice-first service with photo-based prompts and family prompt voting. This shows people pay for capturing stories by voice.
demand_evidence.quality: Low. A vendor claim we cannot verify, but it does show a paid market exists.

demand_evidence.claim: A Storyworth blog post (June 2026) cites AARP's 2026 report: smartphone ownership among adults 50+ grew from 55% (2016) to 90% (2025). That supports using phones as companions for older tellers.
demand_evidence.quality: Medium-low. A secondary citation inside a vendor blog. The AARP original was not read.

demand_evidence.claim: Using phones as controllers for a shared TV screen is now a mainstream pattern: Netflix Party Games (28 Jul 2026) and Amazon Luna GameNight on Fire TV (updated 29 Sep 2026). Families already know the 'scan a QR code on the TV' step.
demand_evidence.quality: Supply evidence only. It shows familiarity with the pattern, not demand for storytelling.

amazon_role: Fire TV (Vega OS, React Native for Vega) is the shared stage. It shows the photo full-screen, the queue of incoming questions and the timeline, and it plays finished episodes. The remote, through TVEventHandler and focus management, gives the host control of the session. Captions follow the system caption style through KeplerA11ySettingsInterfaceTurbo. The phones only capture input.
removal_test: This is a partial weakness, flagged honestly. Without the TV, two people can get most of the value from Willow or StoryCorps on a phone. The TV is indispensable only for the group form: three or more people looking at one large photo together, a host who controls turn-taking from the couch, and replaying the archive at the next gathering. If falsification shows that families of three or more are as happy with a single phone, the concept fails.
wow_moment_45s: 0:00 Grandma taps 'Snap' on her phone and a 1978 print fills the TV within about 3 s. 0:05–0:25 She talks into her phone, and live caption text appears under the photo. 0:25 Two grandchildren's questions arrive as cards on the TV. The host presses D-pad right and OK on 'Who took this photo?'. 0:35 A 'Grandpa says 1979?' conflict chip appears beside the '1978 · Pune' chip on the timeline. 0:40 The TV replays the chapter in her own voice with word-synced captions.
original_mechanism: (1) A question relay: questions are submitted privately on phones and released publicly by the D-pad host, so the elder never sees a wall of questions and the host controls pacing. (2) A multi-teller claim ledger: Nova Lite extracts claims about each photo as structured data (who, where, when, event) with the speaker attached. Conflicts are detected deterministically by comparing year and place fields across speakers. They are shown on the TV for the family to resolve and are never merged by the model. (3) Episode compiler: photo, audio segments, word-timed captions, chapter questions and a timeline, replayable offline on the TV.

data_route: The phone PWA (HTTPS) requests a presigned PUT and uploads a JPEG (2 MB or less) and an audio clip (WebM/Opus) to S3 in us-east-1. An S3 event triggers Lambda, which starts a Transcribe job. On completion, Lambda calls Nova Lite (Converse) with the transcript and photo ID and gets back questions and claims as JSON. Lambda writes to DynamoDB, then sends to the TV and phones over the WebSocket. The TV fetches episode audio and images through presigned GET URLs or CloudFront and caches them for offline replay. All TV traffic is HTTPS/WSS, because Vega WebView blocks cleartext by default and the same policy is assumed for native code (assumption).
auth: No accounts. The TV creates a room and shows a QR code carrying a short-lived HMAC-signed join token (4 h). Each phone must accept a consent screen before its microphone or camera turns on. Roles are host (the TV), teller and asker. Every speaker can delete their own clips. Rooms expire after 30 days unless the family saves the episode. API keys stay server-side.
preview_constraints: The VVD has no microphone, but all audio is captured on phones, so this does not matter. There is no TV camera, and the phone camera is used. The demo needs at least 3 phones or browsers on HTTPS (getUserMedia requires a secure context). Vega WebSocket support must be confirmed on day 1. The video may contain only the family's own photos and voices, with consent from everyone on camera, and no copyrighted media.

This is a new integration pattern, in line with the rules' Open Source creative example.

estimate.assumptions: All estimates. hours_duo is per person when split (TV app vs backend and PWA), including about 15% coordination overhead. Includes 14 h for Vega toolchain, Rosetta and VVD setup, 10 h for the demo video and 8 h for submission writing. Assumes a developer fluent in React and TypeScript and new to Vega. Cloud usage assumes about 300 min of audio in dev and demo. Transcribe batch is $0.006–0.024/min (the digest lists $0.006/min at medium confidence; $0.024 is a conservative assumption), so ≤$7.20. Nova Lite at about 2M input and 0.5M output tokens costs about $0.24 (verified rates). WebSocket, Lambda, DynamoDB and S3 are assumed to stay under a few dollars at demo volume (WebSocket pricing not verified).

blockers: WebSocket support on React Native for Vega is documented only through a WebFetch summary. The CommonScene entrant corroborates it, but it needs a day-1 spike.
Rosetta is missing on macOS 27, so the Vega tools will not run until it is installed.
A new AWS account may have Bedrock quota set to 0 (two forum reports, no escalation path).
Demo logistics: at least three consenting real people, plus authentic old photos owned by the team's family.
Phone microphone permission and HTTPS on a local network during development (use a tunnel or deployed endpoints).
fallback: If WebSocket fails on Vega, use HTTP long-polling with fetch at 1 s. If Transcribe latency hurts the live demo, show live captions from the phone's Web Speech API, label them as such, and use Transcribe for the archive. If the Vega toolchain blocks, build Fire OS react-native-tvos and record on a real Fire TV Stick over adb. The Android TV emulator is avoided because the rules name only a device or the Fire TV/Vega simulator.
falsification_test: One day, two families of three or more people each. Run a 20-minute story session twice with matched prompts: once with a clickable prototype on the TV plus phones, once with a single phone recording (Willow or StoryCorps style). Measure the number of distinct speakers, minutes of story captured and stated preference. If the single phone matches or beats the TV on two of the three measures, the TV is not indispensable and the concept is dropped. Technical kill check on the same day: a phone event must reach the VVD app over WSS in under 500 ms median.
judge_rejection_risks: It can look like another Jackbox or GameNight QR-join app, and QR pairing is common among entrants.
It may read as 'transcription plus slideshow', and question generation is a latent LLM capability.
Remento already turns photos into prompts, so novelty depends on the group mechanism and conflict tracking.
Impact is emotional rather than functional and is hard to quantify. Potential Impact may score lower than for health or accessibility entries.
Privacy and consent concerns for recordings of older relatives and minors.
The demo depends on staged family footage, so authenticity may be questioned.
risk_profile: Medium-high execution risk: realtime choreography across several devices and a demo with live people. Low TV-platform risk, since the TV only renders, takes D-pad input and plays audio. Medium privacy risk (family voices). Low compute cost.

name: WordGlow TV: adaptive same-language subtitle stories
pitch: A Vega OS kids' channel of short, original, illustrated stories. Each word lights up on the TV at the moment the narrator says it, using Amazon Polly word speech marks. Pressing Play/Pause freezes on the current word, D-pad left and right move between words, and OK replays just that word's slice of audio. The app logs each replay and how long the child stays paused. These signals make up the household's 'tricky words', which drive the next generated episode: the target words recur, sentences get shorter or longer, and the highlight pace changes for each child profile. It builds on Same Language Subtitling (SLS), a TV literacy method with field evidence in India.
primary_user: Early or struggling readers aged about 5–9, watching with a parent or grandparent. First segment: English-medium learners in Indian households. Second: US households. Profiles live on the device.
problem_frequency: Daily viewing slot of about 10 minutes, for example after school. This is the target behavior, an assumption not yet measured.
problem_severity: Medium-high long-term (reading proficiency compounds over time), low acute. The paper cited below says 60% of Indian 'literates' cannot read simple texts.
current_workaround: Turning on subtitles for regular shows (the UK 'Turn On The Subtitles' campaign), PBS KIDS Video on Fire TV, phone and tablet reading apps, and parents reading aloud. Subtitles on ordinary content are not adjusted to the child's level, and research suggests engagement drops when the text is too hard.

demand_evidence.claim: UNESCO UIL LitBase (updated 23 May 2024): in India's SLS programme, randomly selected viewers were tested before and after at least one year of exposure. Those exposed to SLS showed significant improvement in reading and writing compared with those who had no access. SLS also inspired the UK TOTS campaign.
demand_evidence.quality: Medium-high. An intergovernmental case entry summarizing programme evaluations, not an independent RCT write-up.

demand_evidence.claim: An eye-tracking study of 136 weak readers in rural Rajasthan watching Hindi film clips found that 70% engaged in unprompted reading when SLS was shown.
demand_evidence.quality: Medium-high. Peer-reviewed (PMC). Measures engagement, not learning outcomes.

demand_evidence.claim: A research summary (10 Jul 2020) reports a PlanetRead 2018 eye-tracking finding: 94% of children engaged with subtitles when the story was at a low reading difficulty, and engagement fell as difficulty rose. The Linebarger 2010 RCT (n=70, ages 7–9) found gains mainly among the weakest readers, and overall differences were not always significant.
demand_evidence.quality: Medium. A secondary summary by a professional teachers' body. Its nuance (weak effects for average readers) is why the design adapts to each child's level.

demand_evidence.claim: PBS KIDS Video on Fire TV has 102,406 ratings (4.4 stars). Amazon's AI summary of its reviews flags 'Functionality' in 542 mentions, 300 of them negative. Kids' learning video on Fire TV is well used but frustrating.
demand_evidence.quality: Low to medium. An Amazon-generated summary of reviews, drawn from the rivals_weartv digest.

amazon_role: Fire TV is the household's daily viewing surface and the place where SLS evidence was gathered. The Vega app renders word-timed text over illustrations, drives a word clock from the W3C Media audio player, handles word-level D-pad navigation (TVEventHandler and FocusManager), respects system caption styles (KeplerA11ySettingsInterfaceTurbo), and labels every word for VoiceView.
removal_test: Fairly strong, with a stated caveat. The evidence base (SLS) concerns subtitles on TV watched habitually, often with family present. Remove the TV and the product becomes a tablet read-along app, a different and crowded category. That move gives up the habitual viewing slot and co-viewing. Caveat: word highlighting itself works on any screen. The bet that the TV drives more exposure than a tablet has not been tested here.
wow_moment_45s: 0:00 A story plays, and each word glows in sync with the narrator. 0:10 The child presses Play/Pause, and the focus ring lands on 'elephant'. D-pad right moves to 'enormous', OK is pressed, and the narrator says only 'enormous'. 0:20 The parent overlay (Menu) shows 'Tricky words today: enormous, whisper'. 0:30 Pressing 'Next episode' opens a newly generated episode (cached before the demo, and labelled as pre-generated). Its title card reads 'Practice words: enormous ×3', and its sentences are visibly shorter: level 2.0 → 1.5. 0:40 The new episode starts with 'enormous' glowing.
original_mechanism: (1) Word clock from speech marks. Polly returns word marks (time, start, end, value) alongside the MP3. The TV binary-searches the audio player's currentTime against the marks to find the active word. Replaying a word means seeking to mark[i].time and pausing at mark[i+1].time, with no extra synthesis. (2) Household-adaptive generation behind a deterministic gate. Each child's replay and dwell signals update a difficulty profile. A Strands agent generates the next episode under explicit constraints (target words, maximum sentence length, share of known words). A readability gate written in plain code, not an LLM, rejects drafts and asks for a rewrite until the constraints pass. Only then are Polly and illustration generation called. Episodes are flagged for human review before children see them.

data_route: The TV sends batches of replay and dwell events (random profile ID, word, count) by HTTPS POST to API Gateway and Lambda, which store them in DynamoDB. A generation job runs as a Lambda-hosted Strands agent: Nova Lite writes a draft, the code gate checks it, and the agent rewrites until it passes. Polly then returns the MP3 and the word-marks JSON, and the illustrations are generated. Everything goes to S3, and CloudFront serves the TV, which downloads and caches the bundle. Playback is fully local: the word clock runs on the device with no network calls during the story.
auth: No child accounts. A random device or profile ID is created on first launch, and the parent overlay is behind a local 4-digit PIN. Only aggregate counts of replayed words are stored: no voice, images or names of children. The backend accepts writes signed with a per-install secret. Content endpoints are read-only through CloudFront.
preview_constraints: Runs entirely on the VVD, with no microphone or camera needed. Timing precision of VVD audio output and currentTime is not documented. The Cinemastamps entrant reports capturing simulator audio, which is anecdotal. All episode content is original and generated, so no copyright issue. HTTPS only.

aws_builder_path: A multi-service pipeline where each service has a clear job. A Strands agent orchestrates generation with deterministic tools: readability_check, target_word_coverage, synthesize_with_marks (Polly) and illustrate. Bedrock Nova writes drafts, Polly provides audio and word timing (the core sync mechanism), S3 and CloudFront distribute episode bundles, and DynamoDB holds the adaptation signals. This matches the rules' 'Creative' AWS example of a multi-service pipeline plus agent orchestration. Development uses Claude Code on Bedrock or Kiro Crew.
open_source_path: Release 'react-native-word-clock' under MIT: a component and hook that turns Polly speech marks or WebVTT word timestamps into a seek-safe active-word index, slices per-word replay, and renders 10-foot highlighted text with D-pad word focus. It targets RN for Vega, react-native-tvos and web, with vitest unit tests for the binary-search clock and drift correction. Also open a PR adding a speech-mark cue source to the MIT-licensed vega-media-kit. This is a reusable Vega-ready integration pattern, not a README edit.

estimate.assumptions: All estimates. hours_duo is per person when split (TV app vs generation pipeline). Includes 14 h for Vega setup, 16 h for writing and reviewing episodes, 10 h for the video and 8 h for submission. Cloud usage assumes about 60 generated drafts and 12 kept episodes of about 1,500 characters each, about 90k characters for Polly. Polly neural pricing was not verified this session; at an assumed $16 per 1M characters that is about $1.50. Nova Lite text costs under $1 (verified rates). Illustrations: about 240 images at an assumed ~$0.04 each (Nova Canvas price not verified) is about $10. S3, CloudFront, Lambda and DynamoDB are assumed near zero at demo volume.

blockers: Precision of audio currentTime and seek on the VVD and Vega devices is unverified. Highlight drift above about 150 ms would undermine the core interaction.
Safety and accuracy of AI-generated children's content. Amazon pulled its own AI Video Recaps after errors (Engadget, 12 Dec 2025).
Consistency of illustrations across pages if Nova Canvas is used. Its availability and price were not verified.
No real children are tested before submission unless parents consent, so efficacy cannot be claimed and only the SLS literature can be cited.
Rosetta and Vega toolchain setup, plus possible Bedrock quota problems.
fallback: If the audio clock jitters on the VVD, run a JS timer started at play() and re-anchor it at each sentence mark. If image generation fails, use simple vector scenes (the react-native-svg Vega port exists). If the generation pipeline is late, ship a hand-reviewed, pre-generated episode set, with adaptation choosing among existing levels instead of generating new ones. If Vega is blocked, use Fire OS on a real stick.
falsification_test: Day 1, technical: build a single-screen Vega prototype that plays one Polly MP3 with word marks and logs the highlight error against the marks over 3 minutes on the VVD. Kill or rework if the median error is above 150 ms. Day 1, user (with parental consent): 3–5 children aged 5–8 watch 2 pre-generated episodes on a TV, word-level highlight versus sentence-level subtitles, while an observer tallies looks at the text and any use of word replay. If fewer than half look at the words or none use replay, or if parents say they would rather use a tablet app, the TV-specific bet fails.

name: BigPrint: a talking TV magnifier where the remote is the shutter
pitch: For older adults with low vision, a spare phone on a cheap stand becomes the camera and the Fire TV becomes the large display of a video magnifier. They press OK on the remote and the paired phone, running a kiosk page, photographs the letter on the table. Within seconds the TV shows the page reflowed at 60–96 px in the viewer's high-contrast colors and reads it aloud sentence by sentence. It also shows a card answering what this is, who sent it, what they want, by when and how much. Every fact on the card has a 'Show me' action that zooms into the exact region of the photographed page, using Textract geometry, so the user can check it. 'Send to Priya' shares the card with a family helper only after an explicit on-screen confirmation.
primary_user: Adults aged 65 and over with low vision who live independently, plus one remote family helper (often an adult child).
problem_frequency: Several times a week: mail, bills, medicine labels and appointment letters. This is an assumption and has not been measured.
problem_severity: High for the tasks affected: missed due dates, medication confusion and loss of independence or privacy when someone else has to read the mail. NCOA reports that 37% of older adults with blindness or low vision have incomes below $20,000, so expensive aids are often out of reach.
current_workaround: Video magnifiers (CCTV): models that plug into a TV cost $400–$1,000, and stand-mounted models with an x-y table cost $1,800–$4,000 (AFB). Desktop units with OCR and speech list at $3,299–$4,998 at one retailer. Other options are handheld magnifiers, phone magnifier or reader apps (not verified in reviewed sources), or asking family to read the document over the phone.

demand_evidence.claim: About 7 million people in the US have vision impairment, including 1 million who are blind. As of 2012, 4.2 million Americans aged 40 or older had uncorrectable vision impairment (CDC Fast Facts, published 15 May 2024).
demand_evidence.quality: High. Government source, although some figures are older.

demand_evidence.claim: 7.3% of Americans aged 65 and over report being blind or having serious difficulty seeing even with glasses, rising to 9.8% at age 80 and over. 37% of this group have annual incomes below $20,000, and 33.3% also have a hearing impairment (NCOA, 1 May 2025, using BRFSS and ACS data).
demand_evidence.quality: Medium-high. A nonprofit summary of federal survey data.

demand_evidence.quality: High. Peer-reviewed.

amazon_role: Fire TV is the large-format reading display and the tactile control surface. The Vega app maps remote keys to camera actions: OK = capture, Up/Down = step through lines, Play = read aloud, Menu = share. It renders reflowed text in the system caption and accessibility styles (KeplerA11ySettingsInterfaceTurbo), zooms into evidence regions, and labels everything for VoiceView. The phone acts only as a fixed camera appliance.
removal_test: Strong. In the existing CCTV magnifier category, a large display is the whole point, and the TV is that display. Remove the TV and the product becomes a phone magnifier showing a few words at a time on a 6-inch screen, which is the pain point of the category. Honest caveat: cheap magnifiers that plug into a TV also use the TV (a Reddit snippet, not read, mentions $60–80 units). Our difference comes from AI reflow, fact cards grounded in the source and the remote-as-shutter design, not from the TV alone.
wow_moment_45s: 0:00 A phone on a stand points down at an electricity bill on the coffee table. The viewer presses OK on the remote. 0:04 The TV shows 'Electricity bill · Due 12 Oct · ₹2,340' in yellow on black at about 90 px. 0:12 Down then OK on 'Show me': the TV zooms into the photographed bill with a box around the amount. 0:22 Play: the reflowed text is read aloud while the current line is enlarged. 0:35 Menu, 'Send to Priya?', OK: a confirmation appears. Under 45 s.
original_mechanism: (1) Remote-as-shutter across devices. A TV key event becomes a WSS command to a paired phone page that keeps a live getUserMedia stream and Wake Lock. The phone grabs a full-resolution still and uploads it, so the older adult never handles the phone. (2) Fact cards grounded in the source. Textract AnalyzeDocument with QUERIES and LAYOUT returns answers with confidence scores and bounding boxes. Nova Lite may only restate facts in plain language using the Textract lines it was given, each with a line ID. Facts below a confidence threshold show as 'Not sure, show me' instead of a value. The TV renders the source crop from the geometry, so every claim can be checked by eye. Account numbers are masked to the last 4 digits on screen.

data_route: TV key OK sends a WSS 'capture' message to API Gateway, and Lambda posts it to the paired phone's connection. The phone takes a still from the live stream and does a presigned PUT to S3 (KMS-encrypted, deleted after 24 h). An S3 event triggers Lambda, which calls Textract AnalyzeDocument with queries such as 'Who is this from?', 'What is the amount due?', 'What is the due date?' and 'What action is requested?', plus LAYOUT. Lambda then calls Nova Lite with only the returned lines and IDs to produce the plain-language card, including line IDs. Polly synthesizes the sentence audio. The result goes to DynamoDB and is pushed to the TV over WSS. The TV fetches crops and audio through short-lived presigned GETs. Nothing is stored after 24 h unless shared.
auth: One-time pairing: the TV shows a QR code and the phone kiosk page claims a device-pair token (HMAC, rotatable). The helper is invited once from the TV with an explicit consent screen, and the helper link is scoped to shared cards only. No passwords. In-app copy states that documents go to AWS us-east-1 for processing. Account numbers are masked on the TV.
preview_constraints: The VVD has no camera, which is by design here, so a real phone is used. The VVD has no microphone, which is not needed. The demo runs on the VVD plus one real phone over HTTPS/WSS. VoiceView on the VVD is supported only by an entrant's report (Cinemastamps captured VoiceView speech on the simulator), which is anecdotal. Demo documents must be the team's own, redacted, or clearly synthetic sample bills labelled as such.
hardware: Apple Silicon Mac with the VVD, one spare phone (Android or iPhone), a $10–15 phone stand and a desk lamp. Optional: a Fire TV Stick 4K Select for a real-device take with the new tactile remote (that remote ships with the US 3rd-gen stick; India availability not verified).

deployment_prereqs: Rosetta, Vega SDK and the VVD. A Paid-plan AWS account. Textract, Polly and Bedrock Nova Lite enabled in us-east-1, with quota checked on day 1. A KMS key and an S3 lifecycle rule. A budget alarm. Keep the endpoint live through 20 Nov 2026 with a judge-test phone page.

Bedrock Nova Lite is limited to restating Textract lines with citations. Polly reads aloud. API Gateway WebSocket carries the TV-to-phone shutter command. S3 with KMS and a 24 h lifecycle supports the privacy promise, and DynamoDB holds cards. estimate.assumptions: All estimates. hours_duo is per person (TV app vs backend, phone kiosk and evaluation). Includes 14 h for Vega setup, 10 h for the 30-document evaluation, 10 h for the video and 8 h for submission. Cloud usage assumes about 500 pages analyzed in dev, evaluation and demo. blockers: Capture quality: glare, focus and skew from a phone on a stand under room lighting may degrade Textract results.

Language coverage: Indian bills often mix scripts, and Textract's support for Hindi is not verified, so the MVP is English-only.

fallback: If the remote-triggered channel fails on Vega, have the phone capture automatically when the page is still for 1.5 s and push results to the TV by polling. If Textract QUERIES accuracy is low, use DetectDocumentText plus Nova Lite with line-ID citations, still showing evidence crops. If Vega is blocked, use Fire OS on a real stick through adb.
falsification_test: One day. Photograph 30 of the team's own documents (bills, letters, medicine labels; redacted) with a phone on a stand under ordinary living-room light. Run Textract AnalyzeDocument QUERIES for sender, amount, due date and requested action. Kill or rescope if fewer than 90% of returned fields are correct or more than 20% fall below the confidence threshold. In parallel, ask 2–3 older adults (or teammates wearing low-vision simulation glasses if none are available, labelled as a simulation) to read the same letter on TV reflow and on a phone magnifier app. If the TV is not faster or preferred, the TV premise fails.
judge_rejection_risks: Fire TV accessibility entries are crowded, and judges may lump this in with audio-description projects.
It may be seen as an OCR wrapper if the grounding and the remote-as-shutter are not shown clearly.
It needs a phone, so it is not literally remote-only, and setting up a phone stand may seem unrealistic for the target user.
Sending sensitive documents to the cloud is a privacy concern, made sharper by the 2026 privacy backlash.
Errors in financial or medical readings would carry liability, and demo evidence of safety may feel thin.
The demo may use simulated low vision rather than real users.
risk_profile: Low-medium technical risk: synchronous Textract plus a simple two-device command channel with a fixed phone. High sensitivity to trust, privacy and accuracy, because the documents are financial and medical. High crowding and collision risk among accessibility entries on Fire TV. Demo risk is low, since one person can record it.

pitch: After a water, fire or storm loss, ClaimTrail keeps the claim's running record for the ~6 weeks to final payment: say expenses and adjuster promises out loud as they happen, snap receipts on a phone, and ask 'what is still owed to us?' to get answers computed from the ledger, not model memory.

name: Said & Done: a two-key promise board for households (Bee + Fire TV)
pitch: Promises spoken at home are captured by Bee and become proposals that carry the verbatim quote. The other person accepts or declines on the living-room Fire TV. Any later change must be accepted again, and an item closes only when the counterparty confirms it is done. This is accepted ownership, not another to-do list.
primary_user: Two-adult households where one adult wears Bee and the other does not, for example working parents splitting school, medical and home logistics. The non-wearer acts through the shared Fire TV with no app to install. Assumption: the household has a Fire TV; the demo may use the Vega Virtual Device instead.
problem_frequency: Inference, not measured: daily. Household promises ('I'll call the plumber', 'can you renew the car insurance?') are made in passing on most days. The falsification test counts real promises per evening.
problem_severity: Medium (inference). Missed promises cause friction, late fees and missed appointments, not safety harm. Related evidence: parents report overcommunication and multi-platform burden (Romper, citing a 2026 systematic review), and Bee reviewers report to-do overload and poor speaker attribution (Forbes Vetted).
current_workaround: Bee's own suggested to-dos and commitment recall, which are single-user. Otherwise WhatsApp or text threads, hand-typed shared lists (Cozi, Hearth, Skylight), or memory. No reviewed source describes a spoken promise becoming an item the other person must explicitly accept, revise and close.

amazon_role: Bee is the only capture source and also the write-back target: wearer-owned accepted items become Bee todos with alarms, and completions are read from the changefeed. The Fire TV Vega app is the shared household screen where the non-wearer accepts, declines, approves revisions and confirms completion with the D-pad. AWS (API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, Bedrock) is the reachable backend between the laptop-bound Bee CLI and the TV.
removal_test: Without Bee, the product becomes a manually typed shared board, which is Cozi, Hearth and Caring Village territory. The core is lost: automatic capture of spoken promises with verbatim evidence, and revision linking. So Bee is indispensable. Without Fire TV, the board still works as a phone web page. Fire TV is a surface choice: it reaches the non-wearer without an install and matches the organizers' cross-device example, but it is not indispensable. Weakness: Bee already extracts the wearer's commitments natively. Our value rests entirely on the second key (acceptance), the revision chain and confirmed close-out. Their absence in rivals is unverified, not proven.
wow_moment_45s: On camera (consenting adults), the partner asks: 'Can you book Riya's dentist appointment before Friday? Her tooth is still bothering her.' The wearer replies at length, ending with 'I'll call them tomorrow morning' (well over 50 words). A cut with an on-screen clock shows the real processing delay. The Fire TV board (VVD or a Fire TV Stick) shows a new Proposed card: 'Arjun to Meera: book dentist before Fri', with the quote and time. The partner presses Select > Accept. The card moves to Accepted, and on the wearer's iPhone the Bee app shows a new todo with a Thursday 9:00 alarm. Second beat: the wearer later says 'they only had Monday', and the card turns amber: 'Changed, needs Meera's OK'.
original_mechanism: A two-key commitment ledger. Each spoken promise becomes a record with an evidence pointer: Bee conversation_uuid, utterance text, speaker label and conversation start_time. Every state transition needs a different party for each key. The speaker proposes and the counterparty accepts; later, the owner claims done and the counterparty confirms. DynamoDB conditional writes enforce this, so a double accept or a self-accept is impossible. A later utterance is linked as a revision by matching counterpart plus semantic similarity, and it reopens the acceptance gate. Privacy is enforced by construction: speakers not mapped to a household member (guests) are dropped before storage, quotes on unaccepted items expire via TTL after 72 h, and a decline deletes the quote. Only wearer-owned accepted items are mirrored to Bee todos with alarm_at, and their completion is read back through `bee changed`, because the stream reportedly does not deliver todo events.

data_route: Bee Pioneer or Watch > Bee cloud processing > Bee CLI on the Mac. `bee stream --json` gives liveness; `bee changed --cursor` every 60 s gives completeness. For each processed conversation the daemon runs `bee conversations transcript <id> --json`, then a local filter drops unmapped speakers. Only the filtered utterance window goes to Bedrock (Nova Lite) for extraction. The daemon POSTs derived records (text, a quote of 25 words or fewer, ids, times, never the full transcript) to API Gateway, then Lambda, then DynamoDB (conditional writes, TTL). The Fire TV Vega app polls GET /board every 5 s over HTTPS, and Accept, Decline and Confirm actions POST back. When an item is accepted and owned by the wearer, the daemon runs `bee todos create --text ... --alarm-at ...`. Todo completion is detected through `bee changed` and closes the loop on the board only after counterparty confirmation.
auth: Bee: `bee login` after Developer Mode is unlocked on the wearer's iPhone. The token stays on the Mac, and the Bee proxy and MCP HTTP endpoints stay on 127.0.0.1 as the docs require. Backend: a per-household secret (32 or more random bytes) is created on first run. The Fire TV pairs by entering a 6-digit code shown on the laptop dashboard, exchanged for a scoped device token that a Lambda authorizer checks. There is no Login with Amazon in the MVP. AWS: a Lambda IAM role grants least-privilege access to Bedrock and DynamoDB.
preview_constraints: Bee's Help Center describes the developer API as still being built. The stream is at-most-once, and one entrant reports it dies after about 43 h with no replay. Todo events are documented but reported as never delivered; ticks show up via the changefeed about 35 s later (entrant report). `bee now` duplicates utterances (issue #3). Recordings under about 50 words are deleted (Amazon staff, forum 45111). Processing latency is undocumented. Speaker labels are anonymous (speaker_1) unless named in the app. Since 23 Sep 2026 new customers sign in with an Amazon account, and `bee login` behaviour for them is not documented. Bulk `bee sync` returns 500s (issue #14). Vega SDK 0.24: the VVD has no microphone, experimental APIs are being deprecated, macOS 27 needs Rosetta, Vega tooling wants Node 18-20, and the VVD can crash under memory pressure.
hardware: Required: a Bee Pioneer ($49.99, ships only to the US) paired with an iPhone running the Bee iOS app (iOS 17.6+), or an iPhone plus an Apple Watch (watchOS 10+) running Bee. Watch ambient-capture parity with Pioneer is unverified, though a forum participant reports the Watch works as a recording source. Android is not viable from India (the app is US-only and a pairing block is reported). An Apple-silicon Mac runs the Bee CLI and the Vega Virtual Device (Vega tools need about 20 GB of disk; 48 GB is free). Optional: a Fire TV Stick 4K Select (Rs 5,499, Vega OS) for real-device footage. People: a second consenting adult on camera.

firecrawl_research_role: Pre-build and weekly: re-check rival features (Hearth, Caring Village, Skylight, Bee app release notes) and Bee docs pages for changes to stream or todo semantics, and scan new public Bee entrants for overlap. Evidence goes into the README's rival table with dates.
aws_builder_path: Real value: the Bee CLI must run on the laptop, but the TV needs a reachable, always-on endpoint. API Gateway HTTP API plus Lambda gives that endpoint, and DynamoDB conditional writes make the two-key transitions idempotent and race-free (no double accept from TV and laptop). DynamoDB TTL enforces the 72 h quote expiry server-side as data minimization rather than a promise. Bedrock runs Nova Lite for cheap extraction and Claude Haiku 4.5 only for revision linking. Build with Kiro Crew or Claude Code on Bedrock to satisfy AWS Builder, and describe each service in the Product Feedback.
open_source_path: An MIT-licensed repo with CI. Extract a small reusable package, `bee-cursor`: an exactly-once changefeed processor (persist the cursor after processing), utterance dedupe for issue #3, and a reconnecting wrapper for `bee stream`, all with tests and recorded fixtures labelled SIMULATED. Also publish a D-pad focus-safe kanban board component for Vega. Candidate upstream contribution: a docs PR to bee-cli about todo events not arriving on the stream, once reproduced.

estimate.assumptions: Estimates, not measurements. Solo means one developer fluent in TypeScript and React Native working about 6.5 focused h/day for 18 working days, which gives about 117 h. At about 122 h, BEE-1 does not fit solo unless revision linking or the Fire TV app is cut. Breakdown in hours: setup (Bee Developer Mode and CLI, Rosetta, Vega SDK and VVD, Bedrock quota check) 10; ingestion daemon 10; extraction and speaker mapping 14; state machine, API, DynamoDB and tests 16; revision linking 8; completion confirmation 6; Vega board app 26; Bee todo write-back 5; consent and purge 5; real-data sessions over at least 4 evenings 8; video, README, friction log and feedback 14. hours_duo is hours per person when two people split the work (one on Vega, one on Bee and backend), including about 15% coordination overhead, so about 140 team hours. Bee hardware shipping lead time is excluded and is unverified for forwarding to India.

blockers: Eligibility: without a Bee Pioneer (US shipping only) or an iPhone plus Apple Watch running Bee, real data cannot be recorded and the project fails the Bee rules. The forum's 'no device / generated audio' answer conflicts with the Official Rules, which prevail.
Developer Mode unlock failed for at least one iOS user, and `bee login` with the post-23-Sep-2026 Amazon-account sign-in is undocumented.
Speaker attribution is reported as poor (TechCrunch, Forbes), which directly threatens owner and counterparty mapping.
The Vega toolchain on macOS 27 needs Rosetta and Node 18-20, and the VVD can crash under memory pressure. This adds setup risk to a second platform.
The demo needs a second consenting adult. About a dozen US states require all-party consent, and EU AI Act Art. 50 transparency has applied since 2 Aug 2026.
Bee processing latency is undocumented, so the live 'card appears' moment may need a cut with a visible clock.
fallback: If the Vega app is not stable by about day 12, ship the board as a responsive web page on phone and laptop and submit to Bee only; the Bee rules are still satisfied. If attribution is poor, the wearer assigns the owner with one tap before the card reaches the TV, which keeps two-key acceptance. If the stream is unreliable, run changefeed-only polling at about 60 s. If no Bee hardware or Watch path is working by about day 5, this concept is ineligible: pivot to a non-Bee track.
falsification_test: One day, with a Bee and a consenting partner. Wear Bee through one evening at home, run the extractor over that evening's real conversations from `bee changed`, and hand-label every promise made between the two people. Kill or pivot if any of these hold: (a) fewer than 3 real two-person promises occur (the frequency assumption is wrong); (b) owner and counterparty attribution from Bee speaker labels is right for fewer than about 70% of labelled promises even after naming speakers in the Bee app (most items would need manual assignment, and the capture advantage collapses); (c) the partner, shown 5 real proposal cards on a laptop mock of the TV board, says they would not bother to accept or decline them. These thresholds are judgment calls, fixed before running.
judge_rejection_risks: It may read as 'a to-do list with extra steps' that overlaps Bee's native commitments and Actions.
Household coordination is a saturated theme (Alexa+ family calendar and Visual ID reminders, Skylight Assistant, Hearth, Cozi, Fambot).
Fire TV may look bolted on, since the board could be a phone page, which weakens the cross-device story.
Capturing a non-wearing partner's speech raises consent concerns that judges may weigh against the idea.
Live-data proof is fragile on camera: processing delay, speaker mislabels and the 50-word threshold.
Scope is broad for a solo builder, so polish (the Design criterion) may suffer.
risk_profile: Integration-heavy and people-dependent: two platforms (Bee and Vega) and two humans. Highest build scope of the three (about 122 h solo, above solo capacity). Consent risk medium-high (non-wearer partner). Idea risk medium, because the wedge rests on rival features being unverified rather than proven absent. Technical risk medium: speaker attribution and the lossy stream.

track: Bee (primary). Education priority use case; matches the organizers' 'on-wrist coaching for learning' and 'Agent Skills' examples.
name: Explain-Back: on-wrist retrieval coaching from your own tutoring sessions
pitch: After a tutoring session or consented lecture captured by Bee, Explain-Back schedules spaced 'explain it back in a minute' prompts as Bee todos. The student answers aloud with the Bee button, and an Agent Skill grades the spoken explanation against the tutor's exact words. It shows what was covered, what was missed and any misconception, then writes mastery back to Bee as facts and books the next targeted prompt.
primary_user: University or college students, and self-learners preparing for exams, who attend 1:1 or small-group tutoring, office hours, or lectures where the instructor consents to recording. The student is the Bee wearer. Answers are given alone, so answer capture has no bystanders.
problem_frequency: Inference: several sessions per week, with review moments daily during term and exam periods. Not measured.
problem_severity: Medium to high in exam periods (inference). Re-reading notes is the default habit, while practice testing has a moderate average effect in research syntheses (weighted mean 0.49 across 5 meta-analyses).
current_workaround: Re-reading notes or Bee summaries. Bee Templates turn a lecture into a study plan. AI flashcard apps (RemNote, Studr, StudyFetch) generate cards from a phone recording or PDF, and students tap or type answers. Spoken explanations graded against the source session were not verified in any reviewed rival.

demand_evidence.claim: Practice testing (retrieval practice) across 5 meta-analyses, 744 studies and 222,708 students has a weighted mean effect size of 0.49.
demand_evidence.quality: Research aggregator (Visible Learning MetaX), undated page. Secondary synthesis of meta-analyses.

demand_evidence.claim: In a 2025 peer-reviewed study, retrieval practice improved performance on never-before-seen application questions compared with other conditions, which supports 'explain and apply' prompts over rote cards.
demand_evidence.quality: Peer-reviewed article on ScienceDirect (2025). Lab experiments, not a field trial.

demand_evidence.claim: Counter-evidence: two preliminary online (Prolific) experiments in 2026 found no significant testing effect despite delayed tests and feedback. The benefit is not guaranteed in every setting.
demand_evidence.quality: Peer-reviewed open access (2026), preliminary, online sample. Contrarian evidence.

demand_evidence.claim: Amazon says many customers first used Bee for 'work and school life' to record 'meetings, lectures', and Bee Templates organize 'lecture content into study plans'. Students do use Bee for this, and Bee covers the summary step natively.
demand_evidence.quality: OFFICIAL vendor statement (5 Jan 2026).

demand_evidence.claim: The organizers' guidance says that for Bee, 'on wrist coaching for learning' is what they are hoping to see.
demand_evidence.quality: Organizer guidance (about 18 Sep 2026). Judge signal, not user demand.

demand_evidence.claim: Constraint evidence: Illinois State University prohibits student recording in instructional settings without explicit advance written consent from the instructor and the written agreement of other students who may be captured.
demand_evidence.quality: OFFICIAL institutional policy (one university). Shows the consent design is necessary, not that all institutions are the same.

amazon_role: Bee is both input and output. It captures the source session (tutor plus student), carries the student's spoken answers (button voice notes or short conversations), delivers prompts as Bee todos with alarms, and stores mastery as Bee facts that Bee's own chat and insights can use. The logic ships as an Agent Skill that runs on the Bee CLI or MCP, as the track rules allow.
removal_test: Without Bee, a student could record with a phone into RemNote, Studr or StudyFetch and type answers. The 'session to questions' half survives unchanged; that part is commodity. What dies is the Bee-dependent loop: hands-free spoken explain-back answers in the same data store as the source session, the context gate (no prompts during a live conversation), and mastery written back into Bee facts. So Bee is indispensable to the explain-back loop but not to question generation. We deliberately cut any flashcard UI so the product is the Bee-dependent loop. Flagged weakness: if voice-note answers cannot be captured reliably (the 50-word threshold, latency, the Watch path), the product degrades into a clone of the rivals.
wow_moment_45s: The student's phone (and wrist, if mirroring works) shows the Bee todo 'Explain-Back #4: why doesn't a catalyst change the equilibrium constant? Answer aloud, about 1 minute.' The student presses the Bee button and explains for about 70 words, including one plausible misconception. Seconds to minutes later (the real delay is shown with a clock), the dashboard shows 2 key ideas in green, 1 missing idea in grey, and the misconception in red, next to the tutor's exact quote and timestamp from yesterday's session. In the Bee app, the todo is completed, a targeted follow-up todo appears for tomorrow 8:00, and a new fact appears: 'Can explain: catalysts and equilibrium (mastered 2026-10-14)'.
original_mechanism: An evidence-anchored explain-back loop. (1) A speaker allow-list (tutor plus student, chosen once per session) drops everyone else's utterances before any model call. (2) A rubric of key ideas is built for each session, each idea anchored to verbatim tutor utterances with timestamps. (3) Prompts always ask for a roughly one-minute explanation, so answers clear Bee's ~50-word processing threshold; the platform constraint becomes pedagogy (elaborative retrieval). (4) Prompts are released as Bee todos with alarm_at by a context gate: no active conversation in `bee now` or the stream in the last 5 minutes, and the student is preferably at a 'study' location cluster. (5) The answer arrives as a Bee voice note (`journal-created` / `journal-text`) and is linked to the open prompt. A grader returns covered, missing and misconception, each with side-by-side quotes from the tutor and the student. (6) Leitner intervals (1, 3, 7 days); a miss spawns a prompt aimed at the missing idea, and mastery is written back with `bee facts create`.

mvp_scope: Session ingestion on `update-conversation` / `bee changed`: fetch the transcript, apply the tutor-plus-student speaker allow-list, and drop all other utterances before any LLM call.
A key-idea rubric plus 5-10 explain-prompts per session, each anchored to tutor utterance quotes and timestamps.
Leitner scheduler (1/3/7 days) emitting `bee todos create --text --alarm-at`, with a context gate that defers a prompt if Bee shows an active conversation in the last 5 minutes.

Answer capture via Bee voice notes (journal events, then `bee journals get`), linked to the most recent open prompt. Fallback: a button-started short conversation of 60 words or more, linked by time window.
Grader: covered, missing and misconception with side-by-side quotes. Results complete the todo, create a targeted follow-up todo, and write a Bee fact on mastery.
Packaged as an Agent Skill (`explain-back/SKILL.md` plus scripts, agentskills.io format) that runs in Claude Code, Kiro or a Strands agent, using the Bee CLI and MCP.
A minimal web dashboard: a concept mastery map with links to the exact source moments.
An evaluation: at least 30 of our own consented answers, human-labelled, with grader agreement reported in the README.
excluded_stretch: A flashcard or tap-to-reveal UI (deliberately cut; it is the rivals' strength)
Classroom-wide or teacher dashboards and LMS integration
FSRS scheduling (Leitner is enough for the MVP)
Echo or Fire TV study sessions
Non-English sessions (Hindi is supported by Bee, but grading quality is untested)
Recording real university lectures without written instructor consent

data_route: Bee Pioneer or Watch > Bee cloud > Bee CLI on the Mac. `bee stream` and `bee changed` detect a processed session, and `bee conversations transcript` fetches it. The speaker allow-list filter is applied locally, and only the filtered tutor and student utterances go to Bedrock for rubric and prompt generation. Rubric, prompts and anchors are stored locally (SQLite). The scheduler runs `bee todos create --alarm-at` when the context gate passes, and the alarm reaches the phone (wrist unverified). The student presses the Bee button and answers, producing `journal-created` / `journal-text` events (or `bee changed`); the answer is fetched with `bee journals get`. The answer plus the anchored rubric goes to the Bedrock grader. Results feed `bee todos complete`, a follow-up `bee todos create --alarm-at`, `bee facts create` on mastery, and a local dashboard update. Raw transcripts stay on the Mac; only filtered windows go to Bedrock.
auth: Bee: `bee login` with Developer Mode, token on the Mac; the Skill uses the stored CLI login (Bee docs say the Skill can complete its own auth flow). Bedrock: a local AWS profile (IAM user or SSO) with least-privilege bedrock:InvokeModel. The dashboard is localhost only in the MVP. If hosted for judges, it shows a redacted demo dataset behind Cognito.
preview_constraints: Recordings under about 50 words are deleted (forum 45111); whether the threshold also applies to voice notes is unverified. The journal (push-to-talk) path is what a Bee contributor recommends for command-like use (issue #4), but Apple Watch parity is unverified. An entrant observed todo alarms buzzing the phone but not the watch. The stream is at-most-once. Processing latency is undocumented. Transcripts 'can be a bit of a mess' (TechCrunch), which matters for technical terms. Bee MCP answers MCP 2024-11-05. Developer Mode is required, and Amazon-account sign-in is undocumented for the CLI.
hardware: Preferred: a Bee Pioneer ($49.99, US shipping only), because its button gives push-to-talk voice notes, paired with an iPhone running the Bee iOS app. Alternative: an iPhone plus an Apple Watch (watchOS 10+) running Bee; the voice-note answer path and wrist alarms are unverified. A Mac runs the CLI, the Skill and the dashboard. People: a consenting teammate acting as tutor for demo sessions. No TV or Echo.
sdk_versions: @beeai/cli 0.7.3 (pinned). bee-skill repo at main (no releases; GitHub detects no LICENSE file, so do not vendor it, reference it). strands-agents 1.57.2 (Python) or @strands-agents/sdk 1.19.0 (TS). PyPI mcp 2.3.0 if an own MCP wrapper is needed. Bedrock Claude Haiku 4.5 for grading and Nova Lite for prompt drafting, in us-east-1 or us-west-2.

AWS account with Bedrock model access validated on day 1. A written consent note from the demo tutor. The repo must show the Bee CLI or MCP actually called at runtime (Skill scripts invoking `bee`), not just named.
firecrawl_research_role: Pre-build: learning-science evidence (practice testing, self-explanation) and rival feature checks (RemNote, Studr, StudyFetch, Bee Templates). Already done: three searches saved as .firecrawl/idea-bee-retrieval-practice.json, idea-bee-lecture-flashcard-rivals.json and idea-bee-lecture-recording-policy.json. During the build: monitor Bee docs for journal and todo event changes.
aws_builder_path: Strands Agents runs the Explain-Back Skill with Bedrock models: Nova Lite drafts prompts cheaply, and Claude Haiku 4.5 grades with structured output. Bedrock batch inference (50% off for select models) re-grades the labelled evaluation set whenever the rubric prompt changes, giving a reproducible agreement number in the README. Built with Kiro Crew or Claude Code on Bedrock. Honest limit: the Bee CLI must run locally, so AgentCore Runtime adds little here, and the AWS story is mostly model hosting plus evaluation. Judges may rate the AWS depth as modest.
open_source_path: Publish `explain-back` as an installable Agent Skill (`npx skills add <repo>`), MIT licensed. It includes the anchored-rubric grader prompt, the Leitner scheduler and the context-gate logic, with unit tests on fixture transcripts labelled SIMULATED. Real transcripts are never committed; only aggregate agreement numbers from consented real sessions are reported. This is a reusable pattern for any Bee-based coaching skill.

The voice-note answer path is unverified on Apple Watch, and whether the ~50-word deletion threshold applies to voice notes is unknown.

With a consenting teammate as tutor, record two 8-minute mini-tutorials through Bee, then give 8 spoken explain-back answers of about 60-90 words each by Bee voice note. Kill or pivot if: (a) answers do not reach the CLI as journal events or conversations within about 10 minutes, or short answers are dropped; (b) the grader agrees with a human rubric on fewer than 6 of 8 answers; (c) fewer than 8 of 10 generated prompts are answerable from the anchored tutor quotes (the transcript is too messy for technical terms); (d) the todo alarm reaches neither wrist nor phone. If (a) or (b) fails, the product collapses into a flashcard app that rivals already ship.
judge_rejection_risks: The AI study-app category is crowded (RemNote, Studr, StudyFetch, NoteHive, Otter, Bee Templates), so judges may file it as 'transcription plus quiz'.
The learning benefit of LLM-graded spoken explanations is unproven, and the testing effect does not replicate in every setting (2026 Prolific study).
Consent around lecture recording may concern judges if real classes appear.
The 'on-wrist' claim weakens if prompts visibly arrive on the phone.
A teammate acting as tutor may look staged unless the Bee app and CLI timestamps are shown as live.
The AWS Builder angle is modest (mostly Bedrock).
risk_profile: Data-path and efficacy risk. Moderate build scope (about 109 h solo) on a single platform with no TV, Echo or second app. The highest uncertainty is in Bee-specific paths: voice-note answers, the 50-word threshold and wrist delivery. Idea crowding is high in the consumer study-app market but low among visible Bee entrants (no education entrant found among the roughly 10 visible Bee repos). Consent risk medium for the tutor or lecturer; low for answers, which are given alone.

track: Bee (primary). Developer-experience priority use case; candidate for AWS Builder (Claude Code on Bedrock) and Open Source mini-challenges.
name: TriedThat: spoken debugging memory that stops coding agents repeating your dead ends
pitch: While you debug aloud or pair, Bee hears 'I bumped the timeout to 30 seconds and it still flakes'. TriedThat turns that narration into symbol-linked attempt records. When you hand the bug to Claude Code, hooks inject what you already ruled out, with your exact words. If the agent starts editing toward a ruled-out fix, TriedThat stops and asks. The pull request gets a cited 'ruled out during debugging' section only after you tick a Bee todo.
primary_user: Individual developers and pairs who debug aloud or pair-program and then hand work to coding agents (Claude Code, Kiro). Solo narration mode has no bystanders. Pair mode requires the partner's opt-in.
problem_frequency: Inference: daily for developers who use coding agents. Agents start each session without the human's spoken reasoning. Not measured; the falsification test measures repeat attempts directly.
problem_severity: Medium: wasted agent turns and tokens, wrong fixes merged, review time. The top AI frustration in the 2025 Stack Overflow survey was solutions that are 'almost right, but not quite' (66%), followed by debugging AI code taking more time (45.2%).
current_workaround: Typing context into the prompt or CLAUDE.md (rarely done mid-debug), re-explaining after the agent repeats a failed fix, or connecting Bee's own MCP to Claude Code (`bee mcp connect claude-code`) and asking the agent to search transcripts manually. That baseline is the main substitute to beat.

demand_evidence.claim: The 2025 Stack Overflow survey (AI section) found that the biggest single AI-tool frustration, cited by 66%, is 'AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite'. The second is 'Debugging AI-generated code is more time-consuming' at 45.2%.
demand_evidence.quality: SURVEY (2025, large developer sample). The vendor blog below swaps the 66% and 45% labels, a contradiction; the survey page figures are used.

demand_evidence.claim: 75% of developers would still ask another person for help when they don't trust AI's answers, and trust in AI accuracy fell to 29%. Human context still matters.
demand_evidence.quality: VENDOR-BLOG summarizing its own survey. Its 66/45 framing conflicts with the survey page.

demand_evidence.claim: A practitioner review of ADRs lists 'The context is underspecified' as the first common mistake and stresses recording why an option was chosen. Rationale is routinely lost between discussion and writing.
demand_evidence.quality: PRACTITIONER essay (12 Sep 2026), experience-based, not measured.

demand_evidence.claim: A Bee owner piped `bee stream` to a server to drive agent actions and found the transcript stream 'too lossy for reliable action automation'. Developers are wiring Bee into agents, and reliability (changefeed backstop) is a real requirement.
demand_evidence.quality: COMMUNITY, single user report plus one Bee contributor reply (May-Jun 2026).

demand_evidence.claim: Builder interest signal: at least 3 visible hackathon Bee repos target developer workflows (kept, ringfence, Mental-Model-Drift). This shows perceived demand but is also the main crowding risk.
demand_evidence.quality: Supply-side signal from GitHub repos (Sep 2026). Not user demand.

amazon_role: Bee is the sole input: spoken debugging narration, processed into speaker-labelled utterances and read via CLI, stream and changefeed. It is also the consent channel: a Bee todo tick approves quoting in a PR, read back through `bee changed`. Optionally, AWS hosts a team copy of derived attempt records (no transcripts) on AgentCore Runtime, and Claude Code runs on Bedrock.
removal_test: Without Bee, developers would have to type what they tried mid-debug, which in practice they rarely do (assumption), so the product has no input. Bee is indispensable as the source. The harder test is removing our layer instead: Bee MCP plus Claude Code already lets an agent search transcripts. If that baseline avoids repeated dead ends as well as TriedThat, our product is a thin wrapper and Bee alone delivers the value. The falsification test is built around exactly this baseline.
wow_moment_45s: Split screen. Left: the developer, wearing Bee, debugging a flaky checkout test aloud: 'I bumped the timeout to 30 seconds and it still fails, so it's not timing. I also flushed Redis, no change...' (60+ words). Right: the terminal runs `claude "fix the flaky checkout test"` twice on the same commit. Run 1 (no TriedThat): the agent's first edit raises TIMEOUT_MS. Run 2 (TriedThat): the first message shows 'Ruled out by you at 14:02 (Bee conversation 6531525): timeout to 30s, Redis flush', with quotes, and the agent investigates clock skew instead. When it later tries to edit TIMEOUT_MS, a PreToolUse prompt appears: 'Matches a ruled-out attempt (quote). Proceed?'
original_mechanism: A symbol-grounded attempt ledger with a deterministic collision guard. (1) A spoken-identifier aligner maps transcribed tokens to the repo's symbol table (tree-sitter or ctags index; camel/snake splitting; phonetic plus edit-distance match), so 'retry with back off' resolves to retryWithBackoff() in src/net/retry.ts. (2) An extractor turns narration windows into attempt records: hypothesis, action, outcome, verdict (ruled-out, confirmed or unknown), symbols, quotes, and Bee conversation id and timestamps. (3) Claude Code hooks: UserPromptSubmit adds matching ruled-out attempts as additionalContext. PreToolUse on Edit, Write and Bash scores the proposed change against ruled-out attempts (symbol overlap plus text similarity) and returns permissionDecision 'ask' with the quote as the reason. (4) The PR provenance section is appended only after the developer ticks a Bee todo ('Share 2 debugging notes in PR #42?'), detected via the changefeed.

data_route: Bee > Bee cloud > Bee CLI on the developer's Mac. `bee stream` provides the live timeline; `bee changed` plus `bee conversations transcript --since` close gaps. blockers: Eligibility: without a Bee Pioneer (US-only) or an iPhone plus Apple Watch running Bee, there is no real data and no valid submission.
Behavioural adoption: many developers do not talk aloud while debugging, so the demo must not look staged and the target user must be framed narrowly.
Transcription of code identifiers may be poor, which is assumed and is why the aligner exists; if alignment fails, the guard is noisy.
Workplace recording policies and teammates' consent for pair mode.
Crowding: kept, ringfence and Mental-Model-Drift already target Bee plus developer workflow.
Bee MCP protocol version (2024-11-05) and stream quirks (43 h drop, missing todo events) need workarounds.
fallback: If the A/B shows the Bee MCP baseline is as good, narrow the product to the consent-gated PR provenance plus the deterministic PreToolUse guard (still Bee-dependent) or drop the concept. If identifier alignment is weak, prompt the developer to say file names (easier fuzzy matching) and retrieve by time window around commit timestamps. If hook APIs change, fall back to an Agent Skill plus MCP tool the agent calls voluntarily, which is less deterministic and must be stated as such.
falsification_test: At most one day. Seed 5 reproducible bugs in a sample repo. For each, debug aloud with Bee for 3-5 minutes (50 words or more), ruling out 2 hypotheses. Then run Claude Code three ways on the same commit: (A) no Bee; (B) Bee MCP connected via `bee mcp connect claude-code` plus the instruction 'check what I already tried'; (C) TriedThat hooks. Count ruled-out approaches repeated in the agent's first 3 edits, and turns and tokens to a passing test. Kill if C does not clearly beat B (for example, B already avoids repeats in 4 or more of 5 bugs), because then the value is Bee MCP itself. Also kill if the aligner maps fewer than about 80% of 30 spoken identifiers correctly.
judge_rejection_risks: Originality discount: at least 3 visible Bee entrants already target developer workflows, and ringfence is mature and evidence-heavy.
May be judged niche: debugging aloud is uncommon behaviour.
A terminal-heavy demo scores weaker on the Design criterion.
If the A/B delta over `bee mcp connect claude-code` is small, judges will see a wrapper.
Workplace privacy concerns about always-on recording at work.
risk_profile: Adoption and crowding risk. Lowest hardware and consent risk of the three (solo narration, laptop only, no second platform). Moderate scope (about 108 h solo). Technical risk is concentrated in identifier alignment and collision scoring. Highest originality risk among visible Bee entrants. Impact must be proven with an A/B against the native Bee MCP baseline rather than asserted.

name: CurbClock: a curb witness and 5-minute wait clock for paratransit riders
pitch: A Ring camera that can see the curb acts as the rider's own witness. When a vehicle stops during the paratransit pickup window, CurbClock starts the agency's 5-minute wait clock on the rider's accessible screen and pages a named helper, who has to accept. If the vehicle leaves early, it builds a dated dispute packet that quotes the agency's own no-show rule. It records observations only. It never gives a verdict, and it never claims who was in the vehicle.
primary_user: ADA paratransit riders with mobility or vision disabilities who are picked up curb-to-curb from a house or duplex where a Ring doorbell or camera can see the curb. Secondary users are one or two named helpers (a family caregiver or personal care attendant) who help the rider reach the vehicle. In practice this is US-only, because both ADA paratransit and the Ring partner path are US.
problem_frequency: Every home pickup. Each trip has a fixed ready window: scheduled time to +30 min at Union City, a 20-minute window at Access Services LA, a 30-minute window at Erie LIFT. Each policy read also has a 5-minute driver wait. Access Services alone reports more than 12,000 weekday trips. How many trips a typical rider takes per week was not verified in the reviewed sources.
problem_severity: High for the rider. Each recorded no-show earns penalty points that escalate to suspension: warning, then 7-, 14- and 21-day suspensions at Union City, and suspension at 6 points in a calendar month at Erie LIFT. A suspension cuts off trips to medical and work appointments. Dispute windows are short (3 business days at Union City; 2 business days after month end at Erie). The rider has no record of their own. DREDF cites the National Council on Disability: riders feel penalized despite their efforts.
current_workaround: Riders wait at the window or curb for the whole window. They phone dispatch; DREDF lists being on hold while checking ride status as a cause of missed pickups. They use agency apps that show vehicle location or send an imminent-arrival alert before the scheduled time (Access 'Where's My Ride', myRTCpara, Pace TripCheck). Disputes are made by phone from memory, while the agency relies on its own AVL and driver logs.

demand_evidence.claim: Union City Paratransit policy (updated 21 Jul 2021): the pickup window runs from the scheduled time to +30 min and the driver waits at most 5 min. Arrivals before the window, and departures within the window without the 5-minute wait, are agency errors and are not counted as no-shows. Disputes must be made within 3 business days. Repeat violations lead to 7-, 14- and 21-day suspensions.
demand_evidence.quality: Primary source (official agency policy, read in full). Shows the rules and what is at stake. Does not show how often wrongful no-shows happen.

demand_evidence.claim: Access Services (Los Angeles) rider guide: 20-minute pickup window, curb-to-curb service, driver waits only 5 min. If the driver is early, the 5 minutes start at the scheduled time. Listed grounds include a driver departing before the scheduled time and a driver failing to wait 5 minutes. Riders may appeal or dispute any no-show. More than 1,000 vehicles make more than 12,000 weekday trips.
demand_evidence.quality: Primary source (agency rider guide, undated page, relevant sections read).

demand_evidence.claim: Erie MTA LIFT (effective July 2023): no-show if the rider does not board within 5 minutes of a vehicle arriving in the 30-minute window. Suspension at 6 points in a calendar month. Disputes within 2 business days after month end.
demand_evidence.quality: Primary source (official agency policy, 2023).

demand_evidence.claim: DREDF Topic Guide 7 lists agency-error cases that must not count against riders: vehicle early, vehicle late, vehicle never arrived, wrong location, driver did not follow procedures to locate the rider. It recommends that dispatchers check vehicle arrival against the window using AVL. It cites the National Council on Disability on riders penalized despite their efforts.
demand_evidence.quality: Disability-rights advocacy guidance. Undated; citations run to about 2010, so it is old. The NCD point is second-hand.

demand_evidence.claim: FTA ADA FAQ: before suspending service, a provider must notify the rider in writing and offer an appeal. Trips missed for reasons beyond the passenger's control are not grounds for sanctions.
demand_evidence.quality: Federal regulator FAQ (undated page). Sets the legal frame for disputes.

demand_evidence.claim: AARP/NAC (1 Jul 2026): 51M caregivers of adults 50+, 74% living with or within 20 minutes of the person they care for. This supports a nearby named helper being reachable at pickup time.

amazon_role: Ring is the independent sensor and the source of evidence. Inputs are motion events with sub_type=vehicle, WHEP live-view frames analysed for vehicle presence and dwell inside a curb zone the rider draws, Event History, and (on real devices) MP4 clip download for the window. The mandatory Ring watermark (logo, device ID, timestamp) stays on evidence frames, because it corroborates time and device. It is masked only for inference. AWS hosts the HMAC webhook intake, durable wait-clock timers and dispute-packet storage. No Alexa or Fire TV integration, to keep scope narrow.
removal_test: Without Ring, what is left is a countdown timer plus the agency's own tracking app, which is the status quo. Both the 'a vehicle is at your curb now' trigger and the rider's own arrival/departure record disappear, and those are the product. Ring is load-bearing. Honest caveat: any curb-facing camera with a partner API could play this role. The indispensability comes from Ring being the camera already mounted at the door, not from a capability only Ring has.
wow_moment_45s: 0-8 s: The rider's tablet shows today's trip: dialysis, pickup 2:00-2:30, driver waits 5 min, per the Union City policy (clause quoted on tap). 8-22 s, REAL: Ring Playground live view of the simulated Vehicle event, with the CC BY attribution on screen. The in-browser detector boxes a vehicle inside the curb zone. The rider's screen flips to a large 'Vehicle at your curb 2:07 - 5:00' countdown with sound, and the helper's phone shows 'Asha needs help to the curb - Accept?'. The helper taps Accept. 22-40 s, SIMULATED (ring-sandbox emulator, labelled on screen, team-recorded curb footage): the vehicle leaves at 2:09:10. CurbClock shows that the vehicle left after 2 min 10 s, while the agency's policy lists departing without the 5-minute wait as an agency error. One tap produces a dispute packet with timeline, two watermarked frames (people blurred), the quoted clause and 'dispute by Fri 5 pm'.
original_mechanism: Policy-as-code dwell evaluation. Three inputs are fused into a vehicle-present interval with explicit uncertainty: (1) the rider's scheduled pickup; (2) a machine-readable version of that agency's published no-show policy (window anchor and length, wait minutes, early-arrival rule, dispute deadline, agency-error clauses, each with its quoted source text); (3) Ring observations. Those observations are a vehicle event that wakes the pipeline, then WHEP frames sampled through chained 60 s sessions, classified by an object detector (car/bus/truck classes) inside a curb polygon. The watermark band and privacy zones are masked, and an enter/exit hysteresis is applied. The interval drives an accessible countdown and a named-helper accept ladder (primary, then backup, with timeouts). On a missed trip, a pure evaluator checks the interval against the agency's own error clauses and emits 'candidate agency-error: departed 2:50 before the 5-minute wait'. It never says who was in the vehicle or whether the rider was at fault. On a real device with a plan, the window clip is downloaded afterwards and the interval is recomputed offline. Each packet records whether it came from live samples or from the clip.

data_route: Live view: the backend POSTs the SDP offer to api.amazonvision.com (server-to-server) and returns the answer to the curb-watcher tab. WebRTC media goes straight to the browser, MediaPipe runs there, and only derived observations go to the backend (timestamp, class, confidence, zone, optional one thumbnail). Events: Ring webhook (real) or ring-sandbox (simulated) goes to API Gateway, then Lambda (HMAC check on raw bytes, ack under 5 s), SQS, the trip engine and DynamoDB. EventBridge Scheduler fires clock and timeout transitions. Web Push goes to the rider and helper PWAs. Dispute packets are assembled in S3 (SSE, lifecycle expiry). Policy onboarding: a public agency URL goes through Firecrawl JSON extraction, then the rider confirms each field. No street footage is stored except at most 3 blurred frames per missed trip.
auth: Ring: the Playground bearer token (30 min) lives server-side only; the docs say all calls must be server-to-server. Production would use one-way account linking with a nonce and refresh tokens (about 4 h access, about 30 d refresh). Webhooks use HMAC-SHA256 X-Signature verification with constant-time compare and dedupe. Riders and helpers sign in with passwordless magic links. Helpers see frames only if the rider turns that on. No face recognition, no plate reading.

fallback: If WHEP fails: run the CV on ring-sandbox snapshots of team footage (labelled SIMULATED), keep real Playground device/status/history reads as the live Ring calls, and document the failure in the friction log. falsification_test: In one day. (1) Technical: capture 30 frames from the Playground Vehicle simulation over WHEP and run the detector with the watermark band masked. Fewer than 3 successful WHEP sessions in 10 attempts, or vehicle recall under 80% on clearly visible vehicles, means the real-Ring CV claim fails. (2) Value: read the dispute sections of 10 more agency no-show policies and call 2 agency customer-service lines, asking whether a rider may submit their own timestamped photos or video in a no-show dispute. If none of the 10 offers a written dispute path and both calls say only AVL or driver logs are considered, the evidence-packet thesis is wrong and the product shrinks to a readiness prompt.
judge_rejection_risks: For an India-based team, most of the event layer is simulated. Only device reads, history and Playground live view are real.
Many doorbells cannot see the curb, and apartment riders are excluded, so the addressable share of riders is unproven.
A camera cannot prove the vehicle was the paratransit van, that the driver tried to locate the rider, or that the rider was ready. Judges may see the evidence as weak.
Whether agencies accept rider-held evidence was not verified.
It may be read as a 'vehicle alert' (the Obvious category) if the policy and dispute mechanics are not shown clearly in the video.
Narrow, US-only population.
Recording a public street captures drivers and passers-by. Mitigated by blurring people and keeping no plates, but still sensitive.
risk_profile: Medium-high technical and simulation risk (vehicle CV on pre-recorded watermarked footage; event layer simulated). High problem severity backed by primary-source policies. Medium adoption risk (agency acceptance of rider evidence unverified). Low platform-policy risk as long as there is no OCR, face or plate analysis.

name: QuietBell: a booking-aware silent doorbell for solo appointment pros
pitch: For practitioners who have no front desk and are mid-service behind a closed door. A press on the shared Ring doorbell is matched to the right booking without identifying anyone. It is routed silently to that one practitioner's wrist or phone, and their one-tap acknowledgement appears on the client's booking link. If the client gives up and walks away before being seen, QuietBell flags it.
primary_user: Solo or small-suite appointment professionals who work behind a closed door with no receptionist and no staffed waiting room: salon-suite stylists, estheticians, massage therapists, tattoo artists, tutors and music teachers in a suite or home studio with a Ring doorbell at the entrance. The secondary user is the arriving client. Clinical practices covered by HIPAA are excluded from the MVP.
problem_frequency: Every appointment, so several times a day for a full book. The number of appointments per day was not verified in reviewed sources.
problem_severity: Moderate. Each arrival either interrupts a session (a knock, a doorbell heard in every room, a text that pulls the practitioner to their phone) or leaves the client waiting without knowing if anyone noticed. A client who leaves unnoticed costs revenue: one salon-suite landlord blog puts a missed appointment at $50-$300, a vendor-adjacent figure with no source. This is not a safety problem.
current_workaround: Clients knock, ring a doorbell that sounds in every office, or text the practitioner. Some practices buy wall button and light boards (I'm Here!, Lobbywizard alert lights) or iPad check-in with silent watch notifications and message-back acknowledgement (TapIn, The Receptionist / Sign In App). Others use SMS queue tools (Waitwhile). Late-arrival policies are written into salon booking rules.
