amazon_role: Ring is the check-in device and the presence sensor. The doorbell press (button_press) is the arrival signal for clients who never open a link. A WHEP frame gives a party-size count with no identity. The end times of motion.human events in history, plus one confirmatory frame, detect a walk-away. Configurations provide privacy zones, which are excluded from analysis. AWS hosts routing, escalation timers and the live booking-link page.
removal_test: This partly fails. Without Ring, a booking-link 'I'm here' button gives most of the routing and acknowledgement value, as TapIn and The Receptionist already show with iPads. Ring adds three things a link cannot: the press itself as check-in for clients who ignore links, the party size, and the walk-away signal. That is a real but narrow wedge, and it is the concept's main weakness. It fits best where there is no indoor waiting room and the door is the only touchpoint.
wow_moment_45s: 0-8 s: One door, two practitioners (Maya, Ravi), two bookings 3 minutes apart, both on a split screen of their phones. 8-20 s, REAL: Ring Playground live view (CC BY attribution on screen) feeds the in-browser person counter: 1 person in the door zone. SIMULATED (ring-sandbox, labelled): doorbell press at 2:57. Within about 2 s, only Maya's screen lights up with a silent 'Likely your 3:00, Jordan, party of 1, 3 min early'; Ravi's stays dark. 20-30 s: Maya taps 'Seen, about 5 min'. Jordan's booking link, open on a second phone, updates to say Maya knows they are here and will be about 5 minutes. 30-42 s, SIMULATED: no motion for 4 min, and a confirmatory frame of team footage counts 0 people. Maya gets 'Your 3:00 may have left (last seen 3:01), text them?' with a pre-filled message.
original_mechanism: Booking-aware routing of an arrival without identifying anyone. An assignment step scores every open ICS booking across the practitioners who share one door. The inputs are time offset from the start (an early/late band set per practice), whether that practitioner is in session now (from the calendar), party size from the CV person count compared with the booking's party size, and whether the booking is already matched. Clear wins go silently to one practitioner. Ambiguous ones go to both as 'maybe yours', and the first acknowledgement claims it. The practitioner's acknowledgement is pushed to the client's booking-link page (SSE), closing the loop the doorbell lacks. A walk-away check fires only on events: last motion.human end older than N minutes, then exactly one short confirmatory WHEP frame. That avoids continuous streaming and cluttering the owner's history. Output is a day log of observed arrival versus booked time, labelled as observations and never as attendance verdicts.

data_route: Ring webhook (real) or emulator (simulated) goes to API Gateway, then Lambda (HMAC check, ack under 5 s), then the matcher Lambda, with booking state in DynamoDB (ICS fetched server-side every 5 min). Web Push goes to the matched practitioner. The acknowledgement goes to DynamoDB and then the client's booking-link page over SSE. Frames are fetched only through the server-proxied WHEP or snapshot path and analysed in the browser. Only the count and timestamp are kept, never images. Clients are shown to practitioners by first name or initials only. Day logs expire after 30 days.
auth: Ring: a Playground bearer token server-side only; production would use one-way account linking and refresh tokens. Webhook HMAC verification and dedupe on meta.request_id. Practitioners use magic-link sign-in. Clients reach their booking page through an unguessable per-booking token that expires 2 h after the appointment. A door sign gives clients notice (no face recognition, no stored images).
preview_constraints: Playground provides one simulated Doorbell Pro and pre-recorded CC BY footage (Package/Vehicle/Motion), which needs attribution and is not a salon doorway. There are no ding or motion webhooks, and history has on_demand only, so routing and walk-away timing must be simulated. WHEP sessions are capped at 60 s on line-powered devices and 30 s on battery devices. Each live view also creates an on_demand entry in the owner's history and may trigger recording, so sampling is kept to one confirmatory session. Tokens expire every 30 min. On real devices, TAKE encryption returns encrypted media and disables the CV features.

No Ring hardware for the Playground path. Optional US-located Ring doorbell with a plan for the conditional real path.

(2) Upstream ring-sandbox PR adding shared_suite_rush and walk_away scenarios. (3) A small 'whep-frame-sampler' utility for one-shot confirmatory frames from a Ring WHEP session, with documented failure modes.

Privacy of clients filmed at a business door, especially for wellness services. HIPAA practices are excluded, which narrows the market.

name: OnAir: two-sided camera-use agreements for in-home workers
pitch: A camera-use agreement that nannies, home-care aides or cleaners and the household that employs them both sign. It names which Ring cameras exist, when live view may be used and for what, and who sees what. During each shift the worker is told within moments when a Ring camera's live view is opened, whether that matched the agreement, and when camera privacy settings change. Both sides get a per-shift receipt. OnAir never stores or analyses video.
primary_user: Nannies, home-care aides and house cleaners working in homes that have Ring cameras; they are the people being filmed. Also the household employer who owns the Ring account, and optionally the agency that placed the worker. US focus, because of the Ring partner path.
problem_frequency: Every shift, which is daily for full-time nannies and aides. How often households open live view during shifts was not measured in reviewed sources.
problem_severity: Moderate-high for workers: loss of privacy and trust, legal exposure around audio recording, and fear of retaliation if they raise concerns. Fi2W reports that 63% of over 100 nannies surveyed by Matahari did not know if or how their employers record their voices. Some workers say they welcome video without audio as backup proof against false accusations. For employers the stakes are moderate: retaining workers, and notice duties that Ring's own content policy places on employers who use workplace monitoring.
current_workaround: Workers hunt for cameras themselves and often stay silent to keep the job (Fi2W). Some households disclose verbally or in a written work agreement; per Fi2W, Massachusetts requires written terms for entering a live-in worker's space and Virginia bans cameras in live-in workers' private quarters. The Ring account holder can see live-view history in their own app. The worker sees nothing.

demand_evidence.claim: Investigation of immigrant domestic workers being recorded at work (published 7 Apr 2026). Cameras, including Ring, are pervasive in employers' homes. A Matahari survey of over 100 nannies found 63% did not know if or how their voices were recorded. Some workers welcome video without audio as protection against false accusations. Massachusetts bars monitoring workers' private communications, and Virginia bars cameras in live-in workers' private quarters. NDWA estimates about 2.2M domestic workers.
demand_evidence.quality: Investigative journalism (Fi2W, 7 Apr 2026, read in full) citing an NGO survey whose year and method are not stated. Moderate.

demand_evidence.claim: Ring's Content Policy forbids apps for secretly surveilling roommates or employees, requires apps to give customers easy access to monitoring activity or access logs, and makes employers who use workplace-monitoring apps responsible for notice to employees and any required consents.
demand_evidence.quality: Official platform policy (undated). This is a norm on the supply side, not user demand, but it shows the concept matches Ring's stated direction.

demand_evidence.claim: Ring's Search Party ad (Feb 2026) drew 'creepy' and 'dystopian' reactions, the Flock partnership was cancelled days later, and the CEO was still addressing privacy fears in March 2026.
demand_evidence.quality: Repeated across news outlets (GeekWire, TechCrunch; via trends_home). Demand-side sentiment.

amazon_role: Ring is both the subject and the data source. The agreement is checked against Ring data: the device list with user-assigned names, device status, configurations (privacy-zone count and motion detection on/off; coordinates never shown) and Event History on_demand records, which the API docs define as user- or partner-initiated live-view sessions. One WHEP frame per camera at signing shows the worker exactly what each camera covers. is_third_party_reviewed lets OnAir show that it never pulled media itself. AWS runs the shift-window poller and the shared ledger.
removal_test: Without Ring nothing meaningful is left. The product is a transparency layer over Ring's own live-view and settings data. Ring is fully load-bearing. Caveat: the same pattern could later be extended to other camera vendors that expose access-log APIs, so the agreement schema is vendor-neutral.
wow_moment_45s: 0-10 s: The aide's phone, with no Ring account, shows today's agreement: Front Door camera, live view allowed for arrival checks, private hour 13:00-14:00, audio pledge, and a frame of what the camera sees (captured at signing). 10-25 s, REAL: on the household phone Dana taps 'Check the front door' in OnAir, which opens a real Playground WHEP session. The aide's phone shows 'Front Door live view opened 14:02 by Dana via OnAir, for an arrival check, which your agreement allows', then '47 s, within agreement' when it ends. The latency is measured on day 1 and shown on screen. 25-40 s, REAL event with a shifted demo clock that is labelled: a Playground console simulation creates an on_demand record not opened through OnAir. Both phones show 'Live view opened from the Ring app or another app during your private hour', and Dana is prompted to add a reason, which goes into the shared ledger. 40-45 s, SIMULATED (ring-sandbox fixture, labelled): Front Door privacy zones change from 2 to 0, and both sides are told 'Camera privacy setting changed'.
original_mechanism: An inverted access log. During agreed shift windows only, a poller reads Event History for on_demand records and diffs device configurations and status against a versioned, two-party agreement. Sessions OnAir itself opened are attributed to the named viewer. All others are labelled 'Ring app or another app' (the API does not say who, and OnAir does not guess). A deterministic rule engine classifies each session as within agreement, outside agreement (time or purpose), or unexplained, and settings drift is detected the same way. Results go to the worker as low-key notices and to both parties as a per-shift receipt they each acknowledge. Changes to the agreement need both parties to accept again. The only media used is one field-of-view frame per camera at signing, shown and never stored (only its hash). OnAir's own media access can be checked through is_third_party_reviewed on every event.

data_route: EventBridge Scheduler starts a Lambda poller only inside agreed shift windows. It makes server-to-server calls to api.amazonvision.com for history, configurations and status, and writes session rows (device, start, end, attribution, rule result) and config snapshots (counts and on/off flags only) to DynamoDB. The rule engine then sends Web Push notices to the worker and household PWAs. Receipts are stored in DynamoDB and both parties acknowledge them. No video, audio or images are stored. The field-of-view frame is streamed to the signing screen and only its SHA-256 is kept. Retention defaults to 90 days, and either party can delete their data.
auth: Ring: the household's Playground bearer token (production: one-way account linking plus refresh tokens) is held server-side and never shown. The worker never touches Ring credentials and needs no Ring account. Both parties sign in with magic links. Signing and amending the agreement requires an affirmative tap from both parties, as Ring's policy requires consent by affirmative action. Revoking consent stops polling immediately.
preview_constraints: The Playground has no Ring mobile app and no owner account, so live views opened from the Ring app cannot be shown; only Playground console simulations and OnAir's own WHEP sessions create on_demand records. The single sandbox Doorbell Pro probably has empty privacy zones (unverified), so the drift demo uses a fixture. The Playground has no device_online/offline webhooks, so status is polled. Tokens last 30 min, which interrupts long shift demos. In production, E2EE devices do not appear in the Partner API at all. Whether TAKE affects history metadata is not verified.
hardware: MacBook M4 Pro for development. Two phones (household and worker). No Ring hardware for the Playground path. Optional US Ring Indoor Cam with a plan for the real path.
sdk_versions: No official Ring SDK; plain HTTPS client (httpx or fetch). ring-sandbox 0.5.0 (Python >=3.11, MIT) pinned, for fixtures and tests. ring-api-helloworld (MIT) as the WHEP reference. Node 20/22 LTS through nvm. web-push library (version to pin).
deployment_prereqs: Amazon Developer sign-in for the Playground. AWS Paid-plan account in us-east-1. VAPID keys. Public HTTPS PWA kept live through 20 Nov 2026. A clear 'not legal advice' notice and privacy policy. For the real path: an identity-verified Ring developer account, app registration with Event History scope, US devices with a plan, and account linking.
firecrawl_research_role: Found and read the Fi2W investigation (worker survey, state rules) and checked the angle against the nursing-home camera discussion. Ring's Content Policy was read from the saved research capture. Together they shaped the agreement fields (audio pledge, private windows, private-quarters exclusion).
firecrawl_runtime_role: None. The product reads only Ring data and data the two parties enter. Scraping law summaries at runtime would amount to unreliable legal advice.
aws_builder_path: EventBridge Scheduler (14M invocations/month free per the pricing page) triggers a 128 MB Lambda once a minute during shift windows; each invocation polls 4 times at 15 s intervals. DynamoDB stores agreements, sessions and receipts with TTL. Lambda sends Web Push. Optional KMS key to encrypt token material. Budgets alarm. Built with Kiro or Claude Code on Bedrock. Value: polling runs only while a worker is present (data minimisation) and costs close to nothing. No model is in the decision path.
open_source_path: (1) Publish a vendor-neutral 'camera-use-agreement' JSON schema with a reference rule engine and tests: windows, purposes, attribution classes, drift rules. It is useful to worker-advocacy groups and to other camera APIs. (2) Publish a 'ring-liveview-audit' library that turns on_demand history plus configuration diffs into a per-shift log, including the measured on_demand latency and the client-side event_types filtering workaround. (3) Upstream ring-sandbox PR adding a fidelity note or option for on_demand delay, based on measured Playground data.

Hours include day-1 spikes, including the latency measurement (6h), Ring client, poller and attribution (8h), agreement model with two-party acceptance and versioning (10h), rule engine and drift detection (7h), worker and household PWAs (14h), field-of-view preview (5h), AWS deployment (6h), tests on fixtures (5h), and docs, video and friction log (10h). hours_duo is elapsed hours per person with about 15% coordination overhead.

blockers: Unknown delay between a live view starting and its on_demand record appearing in history. Records may appear only after the session ends.
It is unverified whether live views opened in the owner's Ring app reach the partner history in practice; the doc says they do.
Reports conflict on the history event_types filter (an entrant says it is ignored; the forum says use the plural). Filter client-side.
The 30-min Playground token interrupts long demos.
Clear 'not legal advice' messaging is needed, so the product does not imply legal compliance.
fallback: If the delay is over 60 s or records only appear after a session ends: change the promise from 'live now' to 'notice within N minutes plus a per-shift receipt', and keep real-time notices for sessions opened through OnAir, which it knows about immediately. If Ring-app sessions do not appear: make the agreement require household live checks to go through OnAir's viewer (weaker, and stated honestly). If the employer-incentive test fails: reposition for agencies that place nannies and aides and would require it as a condition of placement.
falsification_test: In one day. (1) Technical: 20 trials measuring the time from starting a live view (an OnAir WHEP session and a Playground console simulation) to its on_demand record appearing in GET history. A median over 60 s, or records appearing only after the session ends, falsifies the live-notice claim. (2) Demand: show the two-screen prototype to 3 domestic workers or caregivers and 3 household employers. If fewer than 2 of the 3 employers would opt in voluntarily, the self-serve buyer thesis is falsified.
judge_rejection_risks: Unclear buyer: why would an employer install a tool that reports on themselves? Adoption may depend on agencies or advocacy groups.
Can be read as a compliance dashboard with no 'wow' and no AI or CV. Tech Implementation may be judged thin unless the attribution, drift and latency engineering is shown.
It cannot say who opened a Ring-app live view, only that one happened.
Owner-app sessions are documented but cannot be demonstrated on the Playground.
Legal sensitivity: it must not suggest it makes a household compliant with recording or monitoring laws.
Niche user group in a hackathon whose Ring examples stress accessibility, caretaking and business.
risk_profile: Lowest technical and simulation risk of the three: the core loop runs on real Playground calls (devices, status, configurations, on_demand history, WHEP). Highest buyer-incentive risk. Medium legal and reputational sensitivity, which counts in its favour only if handled carefully. Lowest cloud cost.
